answers.brief_reasoning: Loanable funds graph: vertical axis real interest rate, horizontal axis quantity of loanable funds. Upward-sloping supply and downward-sloping demand cross at r1. More government borrowing shifts demand right (D1 to D2), which raises the rate to r2 > r1 and increases the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds.
answers.final_answer: Demand for loanable funds shifts right, so the real interest rate rises from r1 to r2 (r2 > r1).

answers.brief_reasoning: Borrowing costs more at the higher real interest rate. That lowers the quantity of loanable funds firms demand, so private investment falls. This is crowding out.
answers.final_answer: Private investment decreases because the real interest rate rises, making borrowing more costly for firms (crowding out).

answers.brief_reasoning: With less investment, physical capital builds up more slowly. That slows growth in productivity and potential output.
answers.final_answer: Long-run growth slows: lower investment means less capital accumulation, so productivity and potential output grow more slowly (the LRAS/PPC shifts right more slowly).

The text-only table stimulus is also unnecessary and adds little.
